Scaling a beautiful 100 g sample roast into a 10–30 kg production batch is where many roasteries either lock in consistent quality—or start fighting roast…

Why Sample-to-Production Profiling Matters on Typhoon Roasters

Scaling a beautiful 100 g sample roast into a 10–30 kg production batch is where many roasteries either lock in consistent quality—or start fighting roast defects.

On electric fluid‑bed roasters like Typhoon Roasters, you have a different set of tools compared with gas drum roasters: 100% convection, precise airflow, and fully logged automation.

This article explains how to move from sample roasts to full‑scale production on Typhoon equipment without losing cup quality. You’ll get:

  • Practical workflow templates for sample-to-production transfer

  • Data logging practices tailored to Typhoon’s electric, fluid‑bed platform

  • Real‑world examples from Typhoon users

  • Benchmarks for batch size, roast time, and throughput on Typhoon Shop PRO and industrial lines

First Principle: Don’t Copy Curves, Translate Them

Scott Rao, ROEST, and Royal New York all point out the same thing: you should not expect to copy a sample roast curve 1:1 into production.

Even on the same brand of roaster, probes, airflow, and thermodynamics differ. What you can transfer reliably are the sensory targets and the style of heat application.

On Typhoon’s electric fluid‑bed roasters:

  • Sample roasts (50–200 g, usually ~100 g) tell you how much power and development time a coffee prefers

  • Production roasts (2.5–30 kg+) apply that learning through batch size, airflow, and heat application

  • Typhoon’s smart roasting software and logging make those decisions repeatable across operators and days

Think of your sample roast as a sensory blueprint, not a recipe.

Understand Typhoon’s Electric Fluid‑Bed Platform

Before you scale profiles, it helps to frame how Typhoon roasters work.

Typhoon roasters are:

  • Fully electric – no gas lines, open flames, or burners

  • 100% convection / fluid‑bed – beans are suspended in a controlled stream of hot air, not tumbling against a hot drum

  • Fast and efficient – 5–7 minute roast times and around 0.3 kWh per kg on Typhoon 2.5/5/10 PRO models

  • High throughput – up to ~6 batches/hour with no dedicated cool‑down protocol

Typical throughput benchmarks:

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO – 2.5 kg nominal batch, ~15 kg/h; matches many 5 kg drum roasters while using about half the energy

  • Typhoon 5 PRO – 5 kg nominal batch, ~30 kg/h; comparable to 10 kg drum output

  • Typhoon 10 PRO – 10 kg nominal batch, ~60 kg/h; comparable to 20 kg drum output

  • Typhoon 20/30 kg industrial – roughly 100–180 kg/h at 5–7 minute roasts

All models share:

  • Transparent roasting chamber (roasting as theatre)

  • Automated loading and exhaust control

  • Smart roasting software with recipe storage and data logging

This common platform is what makes profile transfer easier: once you learn how a coffee behaves on a 2.5 PRO, you’re speaking the same “language” when you move to a 10 or 20 kg Typhoon.

The Four Levers That Protect Cup Quality

On Typhoon’s fluid‑bed roasters, preserving cup quality during scale-up comes down to four main levers:

  1. Batch size

  2. Airflow

  3. Heat application (power curve)

  4. Development time and end temperature

Typhoon’s own defect guide focuses on these when troubleshooting underdevelopment, baking, scorching, tipping, and overdevelopment.

1. Batch Size

Your sample roasts might be 100 g; your production roasts may be 2.5–30 kg.

On fluid‑bed equipment:

  • Stay within the recommended nominal batch range for each Typhoon model

  • Avoid extremely small batches on large machines (e.g., 3–4 kg on a 20 kg roaster) as airflow dynamics change

  • Use batch size adjustments as a tool: slightly reducing batch size can help a delicate, dense washed coffee develop more evenly

2. Airflow

In a fluid‑bed roaster, airflow is not just exhaust—it is the primary heat-transfer mechanism.

To protect cup quality:

  • Ensure beans are properly fluidized (no dead zones or poor circulation)

  • Use higher airflow in drying and Maillard for clean, even heat

  • Consider modest airflow reductions late in the roast if you’re chasing more body—without baking

Typhoon’s automation adjusts airflow for you, but your profiles (recipes) still define how assertive that airflow is over time.

3. Heat Application

Electric elements on Typhoon machines respond quickly, which makes your power curve a powerful creative tool.

For sample-to-production transfer:

  • Use your sample roast to identify power bands: how aggressively you charge, and how you taper before first crack

  • On production batches, reproduce that shape of energy application, not the exact temperature numbers

  • Avoid long, flat energy segments that can lead to baking and dull cups

4. Development Time

Development time and end temperature are usually the most straightforward variables to transfer.

You can usually maintain:

  • Similar development percentage (e.g., 18–22% of total roast time after first crack for a bright but sweet filter roast)

  • Similar end temperature relative to first crack (e.g., 8–12°C above first crack for a medium profile)

On Typhoon, typical total roast times sit in the 5–7 minute range, so development windows are shorter in absolute time but highly controllable.

A Practical Workflow: Sample to Production on Typhoon

Here’s a step‑by‑step workflow combining insights from Scott Rao, ROEST, Royal New York, Artisan, Cropster, and Typhoon’s own training.

Step 1: Run and Cup Your Sample Roasts

Start with multiple small batches, usually around 100 g each.

For each sample roast:

  • Record basic roast data (time to first crack, end time, approximate development percentage)

  • Cup blind and write a plain‑language sensory target, such as:

    • “Preserve lime acidity and florals; avoid drying finish”

    • “Increase sweetness and body; keep citrus but soften edges”

The goal is to define the flavor destination, not lock yourself into one curve.

Step 2: Log Green Coffee Context

This is the metadata that makes your decisions repeatable.

Use Typhoon’s logging plus Artisan/Cropster (if you pair them) to record:

  • Lot ID and origin

  • Process (washed, natural, honey, etc.)

  • Moisture and density (if measured)

  • Screen size

  • Intended use (espresso, filter, omni roast)

These fields become your comparison baseline when you revisit the coffee or move it to a larger Typhoon model later.

Step 3: Define a Production Target, Not a Match

Translate the sensory target into production goals.

Examples:

  • “Same acidity as Sample #3, but +5–10% more development for sweetness and texture”

  • “Match Sample #2’s clarity and absence of defects; slightly lower end temperature for brighter filter profile”

Then express these in Typhoon‑specific operational terms:

  • Batch size (e.g., 2.5 kg on a Typhoon 2.5 PRO)

  • Target roast time (e.g., 6:00–6:30 minutes)

  • Development percentage (e.g., 20%)

  • Energy shape (aggressive early, controlled taper into crack)

Step 4: Run Two Trial Production Roasts

Royal New York suggests at least two trial production roasts after your sample phase. On a Typhoon Shop PRO, that might look like:

Trial Roast A: Bright, sample‑leaning

  • Batch: 2.5 kg

  • Total time: ~5:45

  • First crack: ~4:45

  • Development: 20% (~1:00)

  • End temperature: ~9–10°C above first crack

Trial Roast B: Sweeter, slightly deeper

  • Batch: 2.5 kg

  • Total time: ~6:15

  • First crack: ~4:45

  • Development: 25% (~1:30)

  • End temperature: ~11–12°C above first crack

Cup both roasts against your best sample:

  • If Trial A tastes closest but slightly thin, you can lengthen development by 5–10 seconds

  • If Trial B is sweet but losing top notes, shorten development or reduce energy in late Maillard

Step 5: Lock and Log Your Production Profile

Once you choose a target production roast:

  • Save it as a named Typhoon recipe with all parameters

  • Assign lot ID and customer usage (e.g., “House Espresso – Summer 2026”)

  • Note intended brewing methods and extraction ranges that tasted best

Repeat successful roasts using Typhoon’s automation and your logging stack.

Artisan and Cropster both emphasize that metadata is king: you’re not just storing curves, you’re storing context that makes curves meaningful.

Step 6: Scale to Larger Typhoon Models

When you move from a Typhoon 2.5 PRO to a Typhoon 5 or 10 PRO, you’re still on the same electric fluid‑bed platform.

Best practices for scaling:

  • Keep the roast style constant:

    • Similar total roast time band (5–7 minutes)

    • Similar development percentage

    • Similar energy shape (early push, tapered into crack)

  • Adjust batch size proportionally to the new nominal batch

  • Monitor the first 3–5 batches closely for:

    • Changes in time to first crack

    • Any signs of scorching or tipping

    • Shifts in perceived acidity or body

Typhoon’s industrial roasters (20–30 kg) are built for no‑cooldown, back‑to‑back operation, so once you’ve tuned your profile, you can repeat it at 100–180 kg/h without BBT complexity.

What to Log: A Typhoon Roast Curve Logging Template

Whether you use Typhoon’s native interface alone or pair it with Artisan/Cropster, a structured logging template simplifies profile transfer.

Here’s a practical logging checklist.

Green Coffee Data

  • Lot ID

  • Origin and region

  • Process method

  • Moisture (%), density (g/L)

  • Screen size

  • Intended product (espresso, filter, omni)

Batch and Machine Data

  • Machine model (2.5, 5, 10, 20, or 30 kg Typhoon)

  • Batch size (kg)

  • Batch number (if part of a series)

  • Ambient temperature and humidity

Roast Profile Data

  • Charge temperature

  • Charge time stamp

  • Turning point time

  • Time to color change / yellow

  • Time to first crack

  • End (drop) time

  • End temperature

  • Development time and percentage

  • Airflow settings or profile markers

  • Power application segments (high/medium/low ranges)

Post‑Roast Quality Data

  • Weight loss (%)

  • Color reading (Agtron or similar, if you use it)

  • Cupping notes (structured descriptors and scores)

  • Brew method(s) used for evaluation

This structure mirrors what Artisan Plus and Cropster support, and it maps cleanly onto Typhoon’s automated logging and recipe software.

Real‑World Use: How Typhoon Users Preserve Quality at Scale

Typhoon’s client roster includes specialty roasteries and café chains in Europe, North America, the Philippines, Qatar, and beyond.

From public case pages and training stories, a few themes emerge:

  • Clarity‑first profiles – Many Typhoon users lean toward light and omni‑roast profiles, especially for washed coffees, to showcase origin character

  • Espresso/filter flexibility – Shops often develop a single base profile, then make small development tweaks for espresso vs filter production

  • Back‑to‑back consistency – With up to 6 batches/hour and no between batch protocol, roasteries can run continuous production while keeping roast curves tight

A typical Typhoon workflow in a multi‑café operation might look like:

  1. Sample roast and cup new arrivals on a small electric roaster

  2. Develop a core profile on a Typhoon 2.5 or 5 PRO in the flagship café

  3. Log and freeze that profile as a Typhoon recipe with full metadata

  4. Replicate the same recipe on a 10 or 20 kg Typhoon in the production roastery

  5. Deliver defect‑free, consistent coffee to multiple locations with minimal retraining

Because all Typhoon roasters share the same fluid‑bed logic, baristas and production teams talk in the same terms about roast style and curve behavior.

Electric vs Gas: Why Typhoon Simplifies Profile Transfer

Scaling profiles on Typhoon Roasters is usually more straightforward than on gas drum roasters because:

  • Heat is pure convection, not a mix of conduction, convection, and radiation

  • Electric elements respond predictably; you’re not juggling gas pressure, burner tuning, and drum speed

  • Beans see even heat across the entire mass, reducing hot spots and contact scorching

From a profiling perspective, that means:

  • Less concern about localized defects when you change batch size

  • More focus on the overall energy budget and airflow pattern

  • Cleaner cup quality at higher throughput

Many roasteries view Typhoon as both a quality upgrade and an efficiency/sustainability play:

  • Around 0.3 kWh/kg energy use on PRO models (roughly 3× less energy per kg than many traditional setups)

  • No gas infrastructure, easier permitting, and lower operating costs

Actionable Checklist: Maintaining Cup Quality When You Scale

Use this quick checklist whenever you move from sample to production on a Typhoon electric fluid‑bed roaster.

Before Production:

  • [ ] Cup at least 3 sample roasts blind

  • [ ] Write a clear sensory target in plain language

  • [ ] Log green coffee data (lot, process, moisture, density)

Trial Production Phase:

  • [ ] Choose two trial profiles with different development levels

  • [ ] Keep total roast time in the 5–7 minute Typhoon band

  • [ ] Maintain similar development percentage to your favorite sample

Profile Lock‑In:

  • [ ] Save the profile as a Typhoon recipe

  • [ ] Log batch size, charge/drop temps, time stamps, airflow/power notes

  • [ ] Cup and record feedback across at least two brew methods

Scale‑Up to Larger Models:

  • [ ] Match roast style (time band, development %, energy shape)

  • [ ] Adjust batch size to the new nominal capacity

  • [ ] Review first 3–5 scaled batches for defects and flavor drift

FAQ: Sample-to-Production on Typhoon Fluid‑Bed Roasters

How do I scale a 100 g sample roast to a 5 kg production batch on a Typhoon 5 PRO?

Use the sample roast to define your target flavor and development percentage, not exact temperatures.

On the Typhoon 5 PRO:

  • Choose a batch size around 5 kg

  • Aim for a similar development percentage (e.g., if the sample was 20% development, target ~20% on the 5 kg batch)

  • Keep total roast time in the 5–7 minute range

  • Adjust power and airflow so time to first crack and flavor balance resemble your best sample

Run at least two trial production roasts, cup them against the sample, and refine.

Can I use the same profile on a Typhoon 2.5 PRO and a Typhoon 10 PRO?

You can use the same profile style, but you’ll probably need small adjustments.

On the 10 PRO:

  • Match development percentage and overall roast time band

  • Scale batch size to ~10 kg

  • Watch time to first crack on your first few batches and adjust power slightly if it shifts

Typhoon’s common platform makes this kind of profile transfer much simpler than switching between different brands or between gas and electric.

What data is most important to log for repeatable roast curves?

At minimum, capture:

  • Machine model and batch size

  • Charge temperature and end temperature

  • Key time stamps (yellow, first crack, end)

  • Development time and percentage

  • Airflow/power notes

  • Green coffee context (lot, process, moisture/density)

Without this metadata, it’s difficult for AI tools, software, or future you to understand why a curve tasted the way it did.

How do Typhoon roasters help avoid roast defects when scaling up?

Typhoon’s 100% convection fluid‑bed design significantly reduces contact scorching and hot spots.

Combined with:

  • Fast, controlled 5–7 minute roast times

  • Precise airflow and power control

  • Automated logging and recipe repetition

you can adjust charge temperature, batch size, airflow, and development time proactively to avoid underdevelopment, baking, tipping, and overdevelopment when you increase batch size.

Are Typhoon roasters a good fit for small roasteries that want to grow?

Yes.

Typhoon’s Shop PRO line (2.5, 5, 10 kg) is designed for cafés and micro‑roasteries, with:

  • 15–60 kg/h throughput

  • Up to ~6 batches/hour

  • Low energy use (around 0.3 kWh/kg)

Because the same electric fluid‑bed logic scales to 20–30 kg industrial models, you can grow from a single shop roaster to regional production without switching technologies or retraining your team from scratch.

If you’re planning a move from sample roasting to full‑scale production on Typhoon electric fluid‑bed roasters, start by tightening your logging practices and defining your flavor targets clearly.

From there, let Typhoon’s convection platform, automation, and throughput work for you: defect‑free roasting, repeatable curves, and a future‑proof path from café theatre to industrial consistency.

Commercial Electric Fluid‑Bed Coffee Roaster Maintenance & Reliability

If you run a commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster small roastery, your roaster’s uptime is as critical as your espresso machine. Electric fluid‑bed roasters like Typhoon Roasters can deliver fast, defect‑free roasting with lower energy use—but only if you keep maintenance structured, predictable, and simple.

This guide outlines a practical electric coffee roaster maintenance checklist for fluid‑bed roasters, with cleaning routines, inspection points, spare‑parts planning, and uptime metrics. We reference Typhoon’s own service standards and industry benchmarks so you can build a reliability strategy that scales with your production.

Note: All Typhoon‑specific data is based on manufacturer claims and published support materials.[^typhoon10][^typhoonservice]

Electric Coffee Roaster Maintenance Checklist (Fluid‑Bed Roasters)

Fluid‑bed roasters depend on clean, unrestricted airflow, accurate sensors, and reliable electrical components. That makes housekeeping and preventive checks more important than periodic gas‑burner tuning.

Industry checklists from Cropster and OEMs show a clear cadence emerging: light cleaning every few hours, deeper cleaning weekly and monthly, and a structured annual review.[^cropster]

Daily / Every Shift (6–8 Hours of Operation)

Focus: airflow hygiene, chaff control, and visible safety.

  • Wipe down roaster exterior and nearby surfaces every 6–8 hours to prevent oil/dust buildup.[^cropster]

  • Empty chaff collector regularly:

    • Cropster: every 2 hours or 10 roasts.[^cropster]

    • Typhoon guidance: every 8–10 roasts or before the bucket is half full.[^typhoonclean]

    • Sonofresco warns that failing to clean chaff after each roast can cause a fire and progressively darker roasts due to restricted airflow.[^sonofresco]

  • Visually check transparent roasting chamber (where applicable) for unusual smoke, residue, or uneven bean agitation.

  • Confirm cooling tray is clear of bean fragments, chaff, and debris.

  • Listen for abnormal fan or motor sounds—grinding, squealing, or rattling can signal bearings or motor issues.

For a commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster for small scale roastery, these daily steps are often handled by baristas or production techs between batches.

Weekly Tasks (Every 3–5 Days of Heavy Use)

Focus: deeper cleaning and early wear detection.

Many roastery checklists recommend the following every 3–5 days of production.[^cropster]

  • Vacuum under cooling tray and interior compartments:

    • Use a dry vacuum with at least 15–20 kPa suction and fine‑dust filtration to handle chaff and coffee particles.

  • Clean ducts and accessible airflow paths to remove lint and chaff buildup.

  • Blow out motors and fans:

    • Use dry compressed air at moderate pressure (e.g., 4–6 bar) to clear dust without damaging bearings.

  • Lubricate moving parts (where manufacturer recommends), such as mechanical linkages or door hinges.

  • Inspect bolts, brackets, and fasteners for looseness or vibration marks.

  • Check cable strain reliefs and connectors for visible wear, discoloration, or heat damage.

Typhoon’s maintenance philosophy emphasizes keeping a written log for these tasks and recording any unusual observations before they become failures.[^typhoonclean]

Monthly Tasks (Every 4 Weeks)

Focus: roaster‑level cleaning and sensor accuracy.

Cropster’s reference checklist suggests a monthly deep clean and component review for commercial roasters.[^cropster]

  • Degrease roaster surfaces and accessible interior panels:

    • Use non‑corrosive, electronics‑safe degreasers (e.g., isopropyl alcohol 70–90% on metal surfaces away from plastics; manufacturer‑approved food‑grade cleaners elsewhere).

    • Avoid strong alkaline or acidic cleaners near sensors, wiring, and control panels.

  • Clean fans, ducts, and chaff collector walls to maintain optimal airflow.

  • Clean cooling tray screens and bins so beans cool consistently.

  • Replace or clean air filters according to OEM guidance.

  • Check thermocouples and temperature sensors:

    • For most specialty roasters, Type K thermocouples are standard.

    • Aim for calibration within ±1–2 °C across the typical roast curve range (say 150–230 °C).

    • If readings drift more than 3–5 °C from reference instruments or known profile behavior, plan a replacement.

Typhoon roasters use multiple thermocouples to control fully electric, 100% convection roasting, so sensor accuracy is a key part of repeatability.[^typhoon10]

Annual Tasks (Or Every 2000–2500 Roast Cycles)

Focus: uptime, safety, and long‑term reliability.

Industry guidance recommends a full roastery deep clean and safety review at least once per year.[^cropster][^loring]

  • Full deep clean of roaster and exhaust path:

    • Remove panels as allowed by OEM guidelines.

    • Vacuum and wipe all accessible interior surfaces.

  • Check all thermocouples and wiring harnesses for insulation cracks, corrosion, or loose terminals.

  • Inspect control electronics:

    • Solid State Relays (SSRs) typically rated 25–40 A at appliance voltage.

    • Contactors suitable for the roaster’s heater load (often 3‑phase, 20–60 A depending on size).

    • Inspect for discoloration, cracked casings, or heat damage.

  • Test safety systems (emergency stop, over‑temperature cut‑outs, door interlocks).

  • Retrain staff on the preventative maintenance schedule for coffee roaster equipment and update logs.

OEMs like Diedrich and Coffee Crafters increasingly productize this annual care via toolkits and critical spare parts kits.[^diedrich][^coffeecrafters]

Fluid‑Bed Roaster Cleaning Procedure & Preventative Maintenance Schedule

A fluid‑bed roaster relies on a high‑velocity stream of hot air to suspend and heat the beans evenly. Any restriction in that airflow—especially chaff buildup—directly impacts roast quality and safety.

Core Fluid‑Bed Roaster Cleaning Procedure

A simple, repeatable cleaning procedure keeps your roaster at peak without consuming your entire day.

  1. Power down and cool the machine before any internal cleaning.

  2. Empty chaff collector:

    • After each batch or every few batches, depending on OEM guidance.

    • Never let chaff exceed half the collector’s volume for safety and consistent airflow.[^typhoonclean]

  3. Vacuum roasting chamber surroundings:

    • Use a non‑conductive nozzle; avoid direct contact with sensors.

  4. Clean cooling tray and screens:

    • Brush off loose chaff and residue.

    • Vacuum underneath cooling tray as needed.

  5. Wipe interior viewing windows:

    • Soft cloth and OEM‑approved cleaner to maintain visibility for profile monitoring.

  6. Inspect fan intakes and grills for lint, dust, or obstructions.

Sonofresco’s documentation highlights the risk: failing to clean chaff collector after each roast can cause fires and progressively darker roasts from restricted airflow.[^sonofresco]

Recommended Preventative Maintenance Schedule

You can combine industry benchmarks with Typhoon’s own maintenance philosophy to build a schedule tailored to your throughput.

A practical starting point for a busy small roastery:

  • Light cleaning: every shift (6–8 hours).

  • Chaff collector empty: every 2 hours or 8–10 roasts.

  • Weekly inspection and cleaning: 3–5 days of operation.

  • Monthly deep clean and sensor check: every 4 weeks.

  • Annual safety and reliability review.

Typhoon encourages keeping a written log split into daily/weekly/monthly/yearly entries, plus notes on odd sounds or unexpected cup results, to catch issues early.[^typhoonclean]

Spare Parts Strategy for Commercial Fluid‑Bed Coffee Roasters

Even the best electric commercial coffee roaster will experience wear on electrical components over time. Planning a spare‑parts list keeps you ahead of failures and protects your uptime.

Core Roaster Spare Parts List

OEMs like Coffee Crafters sell “critical spare parts” kits covering the components most likely to fail in everyday service.[^coffeecrafters]

Typical spares for fluid‑bed roasters include:

  • Solid State Relays (SSRs)

    • Current rating: often 25–40 A at mains voltage.

    • Keep at least one spare per major heater circuit.

  • Contactors

    • Sized for heater and blower motor loads (commonly 3‑phase, 20–60 A).

  • Heater elements

    • OEM‑specific wattage; having one replacement set for primary elements can prevent multi‑day downtime.

  • Thermocouples and temperature probes

    • Extra Type K probes and thermocouple wire for bean and exhaust sensors.

  • Blower motors and capacitors

    • For key fans delivering fluid‑bed airflow.

  • Switches and potentiometers

    • Rocker switches and control knobs used frequently.

  • Fuses and breakers

    • OEM‑specified ratings for fast replacement.

Coffee Crafters’ kits include combinations of SSRs, contactors, motor brushes, thermocouple wire/probes, rocker switches, potentiometers, fuses, and heating elements.[^coffeecrafters]

Typhoon roasters use high‑quality European components and are tested against a 48‑point checklist before shipment, but a structured spare‑parts inventory still safeguards production.[^typhoon10]

In‑House vs OEM‑Managed Maintenance

  • In‑house:

    • Daily and weekly cleaning.

    • Visual inspections, basic electrical component replacement (SSRs, switches, thermocouples) when trained.

  • OEM‑managed:

    • Complex electrical troubleshooting.

    • Software or automation issues.

    • Structural repairs or major mechanical replacements.

Typhoon supports operators with remote troubleshooting, spare parts dispatch, and on‑site technicians when needed.[^typhoonservice]

Typhoon Roasters: Service Standards & Reliability Claims

Typhoon positions its fully electric convection platform as a high‑throughput, low‑downtime alternative to traditional gas drum roasters.[^typhoon10][^typhoonservice]

Typhoon 10 PRO Example (Manufacturer Claims)

The Typhoon 10 PRO is a mid‑scale commercial fluid‑bed roaster designed for growing roasteries.[^typhoon10]

Key manufacturer‑stated data:

  • Capacity: 10 kg nominal batch size.

  • Throughput: up to 6 batches/hour, about 60 kg/h continuous production with no between‑batch cool‑down protocol.

  • Energy use: around 0.3 kWh per kg roasted.

  • Quality control: 48 quality tests before shipment.

All of these figures are Typhoon OEM claims based on their published product information.[^typhoon10]

Typhoon Support & Service Model (Manufacturer Claims)

Typhoon’s service program is designed to minimize downtime rather than just sell hardware.[^typhoonservice]

Published support standards include:

  • Two‑year warranty on roasters.

  • Remote troubleshooting as the first support step.

  • Spare parts shipment when remote diagnosis identifies component failure.

  • On‑site technician within 5–10 business days if remote help doesn’t resolve the issue.

  • Complimentary roastmaster training course during installation and calibration.

  • Around 50+ professionals per year graduating from the Typhoon Roastmaster program.[^typhoonservice]

Typhoon emphasizes that every roaster meets CE standards and uses high‑quality European components.[^typhoonservice]

Regional note: service response times, installation requirements, and exhaust/vent permits vary by country and city. Always confirm local regulations and Typhoon’s region‑specific service commitments when planning your roastery.

Uptime Metrics for Commercial Coffee Roaster Reliability

Reliability is no longer a vague feeling; it’s an operational KPI. Concepts like Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and availability help you quantify how well your roasting line is performing.

Definitions You Can Use

  • Availability: uptime ÷ (uptime + downtime).

    • NASA illustrates this with simple math and examples.[^nasa]

  • MTBF: average time a repairable asset operates before failing.[^ibm]

A food manufacturing case study focused on a specialty coffee roasting facility showed that predictive analytics lifted equipment uptime to 97% and cut unplanned downtime by 81%.[^ifactory]

At different availability levels, monthly downtime looks like this for a 30‑day month:[^nasa]

  • 97% availability ≈ 21.6 hours downtime/month.

  • 99% availability ≈ 7.2 hours downtime/month.

  • 99.5% availability ≈ 3.6 hours downtime/month.

  • 99.9% availability ≈ 0.72 hours downtime/month.

For a roastery running 8–10 hours per day, gaining back 15–20 hours of uptime each month can easily justify investment in maintenance routines, spare‑parts kits, and better monitoring.

Actionable Steps for Growing Roasteries Using Electric Fluid‑Bed Roasters

If you’re scaling from a café‑level Typhoon Shop PRO to a 10–30 kg industrial roaster, a consistent maintenance playbook keeps your flavor and reliability aligned.

Practical steps:

  1. Document your electric coffee roaster maintenance checklist clearly.

  2. Build a spare‑parts shelf with SSRs, probes, switches, and a heater set.

  3. Train staff on daily/weekly cleaning and basic sensor checks.

  4. Track uptime and downtime per month so you can spot trends.

  5. Set escalation rules: what your team fixes vs when you call Typhoon or your OEM.

Typhoon’s combination of electric fluid‑bed technology, transparent chambers, automation, and structured service makes it a strong candidate for reliability‑focused roasteries that want both speed and consistency.[^typhoon10][^typhoonservice]

FAQ: Electric Fluid‑Bed Roaster Maintenance & Typhoon Reliability

Q1. How often should I perform a preventative maintenance schedule for a coffee roaster?

You should follow a layered schedule:

  • Every shift (6–8 hours): wipe surfaces, check airflow, empty chaff.[^cropster][^typhoonclean]

  • Every 3–5 days: vacuum under cooling tray, clean ducts and motors, inspect for loose parts.[^cropster]

  • Every 4 weeks: degrease surfaces, clean fans and filters, verify thermocouple accuracy.[^cropster]

  • Annually: deep clean, check wiring and control electronics, retrain staff.[^cropster][^loring]

Adjust frequency upward if you roast continuously or handle oily/dark roasts.

Q2. What are common failure modes on a commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster?

Typical issues include:

  • Thermocouple drift or failure, leading to unstable profiles or inaccurate bean temperature.

  • SSR or contactor failure, causing heaters not to energize or remain stuck on.

  • Blower motor problems, which directly affect fluid‑bed airflow and roast evenness.

  • Chaff blockage, which can cause uneven roasts, darker than intended profiles, or in extreme cases, fires.[^sonofresco]

Having spares and monitoring sounds, roast curves, and airflow helps catch these early.

Q3. How can I tell when a thermocouple is out of spec?

Signs that a thermocouple needs replacement:

  • Your usual profile reaches first crack much earlier or later without any recipe changes.

  • Bean temperature readings jump or show noise compared to stable historical curves.

  • Calibration against a reference (e.g., a known‑accurate handheld thermometer) shows more than 3–5 °C deviation over the roast range.

If you see these symptoms, replace the probe with a new Type K thermocouple and retest profiles.[^cropster]

Q4. When should I call OEM service vs handling an in‑house repair?

Handle in‑house when:

  • You’re cleaning, tightening fasteners, or replacing simple parts like switches or chaff buckets.

  • You’re swapping clearly identified plug‑in components (e.g., probes) with OEM‑supplied parts.

Call OEM service when:

  • You suspect wiring, control board, or automation software issues.

  • Multiple components fail at once or diagnostics are unclear.

  • Safety systems (emergency stop, over‑temperature protection) misbehave.

Typhoon offers remote troubleshooting first and can send a technician on‑site within 5–10 business days if needed, according to its published service standards.[^typhoonservice]

By structuring your cleaning routines, inspections, and spare‑parts strategy—and leveraging OEM service like Typhoon’s—you can keep your electric fluid‑bed roaster running at peak, protect your flavor, and turn reliability into a measurable competitive advantage.

Meta description: Customer-facing roastery design tips to turn your coffee roaster into a brand stage. Learn layouts, lighting, storytelling, and how Typhoon’s visible electric roasters elevate the guest experience.

Why Customer‑Facing Roastery Design Matters

Customer‑facing roastery design is no longer a niche idea. Award‑winning cafés and roasteries now treat roasting as part of the experience, not just back‑of‑house production.

Architectural projects from brands like Common Room Roasters and Blue Bottle highlight glass‑walled roasting rooms and layouts that let guests see into the production flow. Design features often include:

  • Steel and glass partitions that expose roasting while keeping workflows controlled (Common Room Roasters, SCA Design).

  • Roastery zones visible from every corner of the café through full‑height glazing (Paga Café, Dezeen).

  • Glass floors or overhead panels that visually connect roastery and café levels (Blue Bottle Tokyo, Dezeen).

Typhoon Roasters fits this movement particularly well.

Their electric, commercial fluid‑bed coffee roasters are compact, visually open, and designed for in‑shop use—making it easier to position the machine as a centerpiece rather than hiding it in a back room (Typhoon 10 PRO, Typhoon 2.5 PRO).

Best Electric Commercial Coffee Roaster for Specialty Cafés

If you’re planning a customer‑facing roastery, the choice of equipment is a design decision as much as a production one. Many operators now search specifically for the best electric commercial coffee roaster for specialty cafés rather than defaulting to gas drums.

Typhoon’s platform is built around fully electric, 100% convection (fluid‑bed) roasting:

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO

    • Up to 15 kg/h throughput, comparable to many traditional 5 kg drum roasters in effective output.

    • Around 6 batches/hour in the 5–7 minute roast range.

    • Manufacturer‑stated energy consumption of ~0.3 kWh per kg roasted (Typhoon 2.5 PRO specs).

  • Typhoon 10 PRO

    • Up to 60 kg/h throughput with 6 batches/hour.

    • Typical roast duration 5–7 minutes.

    • Approx. 0.3 kWh/kg energy use and a footprint Typhoon reports as 25% smaller and 20% lighter than the previous generation (Typhoon 10 PRO specs).

Typhoon positions these machines as alternatives to gas drum roasters in the 2.5–10 kg class, with a focus on:

  • Even heat distribution from 100% convection (fluid‑bed) roasting.

  • Fully electric operation (no gas lines or open flame).

  • Transparent roasting chambers that invite guests to watch the process.

Energy comparison note: Typhoon states ~0.3 kWh/kg energy use for its PRO series. Many legacy gas drum setups—especially when accounting for burner efficiency, exhaust, and afterburners—are reported in trade conversations and manufacturer data in the ~0.8–1.0+ kWh/kg equivalent range once gas is converted to kWh. Using 0.9 kWh/kg as a typical benchmark, 0.3 kWh/kg represents roughly one‑third of that figure (i.e., about 3× lower consumption per kg). Actual values will vary by model and installation, so roasteries should compare against their own baselines.

Electric Coffee Roaster vs Gas Drum: Which Is Right for Your Roastery?

Designing a customer‑facing roastery forces you to think beyond flavor alone. Equipment choice affects your floor plan, ventilation, storytelling, and operating costs.

Core differences that impact design

When comparing an electric coffee roaster vs gas drum roastery startup setup, consider these factors:

  • Infrastructure

    • Gas drum roasters typically require gas lines, flues, and often afterburners.

    • Electric roasters like Typhoon can simplify permitting and installation in multi‑tenant buildings, though they still need appropriate exhaust and electrical capacity.

  • Footprint and placement

    • Traditional drums often have larger bodies, external cyclones, and cooling trays that push them into back‑of‑house spaces.

    • Typhoon’s transparent chamber and compact bodies were designed from 2017 onward specifically for cafés and small roasteries (Typhoon history).

  • Guest experience

    • Electric fluid‑bed roasters can run cleaner and quieter in many cases, making them better candidates for front‑of‑house placement.

    • Visual elements—like Typhoon’s glass roasting chambers—give guests a direct line of sight to the bean movement and color change.

For many specialty cafés that want roasting as theatre, an electric commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster for small‑scale roastery work is often easier to integrate into front‑of‑house than a traditional gas drum.

Commercial Fluid‑Bed Coffee Roaster Recommendations for Small Roasteries

If you run a single café or a small chain, you may not need an industrial plant. You need a compact, commercial fluid‑bed coffee roaster that fits your bar flow.

Typhoon positions the Shop PRO line for exactly this segment:

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO — for cafés roasting 10–15 kg/h.

  • Typhoon 5 PRO — for shops and micro‑roasteries stepping up to higher volumes (specs available on Typhoon’s site).

From a design perspective, these roasters work as a centerpiece because:

  • The roasting chamber is elevated and transparent, inviting guests to watch.

  • The overall height and footprint are suitable for positioning near the bar.

  • The electric, semi‑enclosed design supports use inside customer areas, subject to local code and ventilation.

For larger production spaces with a tasting room or showroom café, the Typhoon 10 PRO and industrial models enable 60–100 kg/h continuous workflows while still maintaining visual appeal.

Turning Your Roaster Into the Centerpiece of the Café

To treat your roaster as a brand stage, you need to design the entire experience around visibility and storytelling.

1. Layout: Where to Put the Roaster

Customer‑facing roastery layouts around the world share a few patterns:

  • Glass partitions

    • Place the roaster in a semi‑separate room behind a glass wall.

    • Guests can see everything without entering the production area.

    • Case studies: Paga Café’s roastery visible from every corner through glass (Dezeen); Sputnik Coffee’s 25‑foot glass wall showing their 60 kg roaster and silos (Perfect Daily Grind).

  • Adjacent roastery zone

    • If you have limited space, put the roaster immediately adjacent to the bar with a half‑height glass screen.

    • Guests see charge, first crack, and drop without crowding the operator.

    • PDG recommends this layout specifically for adding a roaster to an existing shop (Perfect Daily Grind).

  • Tasting‑room alignment

    • Place the roaster so guests can move from “see the roast” to “taste the cup” in a straight line.

    • Many experiential spaces use a front tasting bar and a back production room separated by glass (e.g., DAK Coffee Roasters’ Amsterdam showroom, Dezeen).

For Typhoon installations, common layout ideas include:

  • Placing a Typhoon 2.5 PRO or 5 PRO directly behind the espresso bar with a full‑height glass screen.

  • Using a Typhoon 10 PRO in a side room with a large viewing window and overhead mirror so guests can see charge and drop.

2. Lighting: Make Roasting the Visual Focus

Lighting can make or break your customer‑facing roastery. Retail lighting research recommends layered illumination—ambient, task, accent, and decorative—to guide attention rather than relying on a single light source (ConTech Retail Lighting Guide).

For your roaster:

  • Ambient light

    • Ensure general lighting is even and comfortable.

    • Avoid harsh overhead glare on the glass roasting chamber.

  • Task lighting

    • Provide bright, targeted light over control panels and sample triers.

    • This keeps operators safe and precise.

  • Accent lighting

    • Install focused lighting that highlights the roasting chamber.

    • For Typhoon roasters, accent lighting on the transparent drum emphasizes the floating bean bed.

  • Decorative lighting

    • Use pendants or wall fixtures to frame the roaster visually.

    • Think of it as a stage: the roaster is the performer; decorative lighting is the proscenium.

3. Storytelling: From Bean to Stage

Visible equipment is only half the story. The way you frame roasting determines whether guests simply watch or truly understand.

A few storytelling tools:

  • Signage and infographics

    • Create a short "From Bean to Roast" panel explaining:

      • Origin and variety.

      • Roast profile (time, temperature milestones in simple terms).

      • Flavor expectations.

    • The SCA notes that origin stories and information significantly influence perceived flavor, even among professionals (SCA storytelling article).

  • Scheduled roast demos

    • Host daily or weekly roast sessions where a roaster narrates the process.

    • Use Typhoon’s automation and recipe storage to maintain consistency while freeing bandwidth for explanation.

  • QR codes on the glass or roaster area

    • Link to videos of your sourcing trips.

    • Share an interactive roast curve for a featured coffee.

    • Connect to a webshop product page.

  • Talking points for staff

    • Train baristas to explain in simple language:

      • What fluid‑bed roasting is.

      • Why your roastery chose electric roasting.

      • How this impacts flavor and sustainability.

Transparency, Sustainability, and Guest Trust

Guest expectations around transparency and sustainability are rising.

  • Deloitte’s 2024 Coffee Study (7,000 coffee drinkers across 13 countries) found sustained growth in demand for sustainable coffee and highlighted closer links between roasters and consumers via direct trade and e‑commerce (Deloitte Coffee Study 2024).

  • The Global Coffee Platform reported that sustainable coffee purchases by 11 major roasters/retailers grew more than 170% since 2018, reaching 1,738,800 metric tons in 2024. These purchases represented 75% of their total reported purchases and 21% of global green coffee exports in 2023/24 (Global Coffee Platform 2024 report).

  • MIT Sloan summarised a study of 467 participants showing that supply chain visibility increased trust and even sales. In one poll, 75% of respondents said transparency supports trust, but 81% of companies lacked full visibility (MIT Sloan, “Supply chain visibility boosts consumer trust”).

Customer‑facing roastery design taps directly into these expectations:

  • Guests can see real production, not just branding.

  • You can connect your electric, fluid‑bed roasting to measurable sustainability actions (e.g., kWh/kg, no gas lines).

  • Transparent equipment like Typhoon’s roasters reinforces your narrative of openness.

Typhoon Roasters — Reviews & Testimonials

Many roasteries evaluating Typhoon Roasters coffee equipment search for Typhoon Roasters coffee roaster reviews and independent feedback.

While detailed testimonials vary by region, consistent themes from publicly available case stories and trade show feedback include:

  • Consistency and control

    • Operators highlight the ability to store and repeat roast recipes.

    • Typhoon’s automation and fully electric heating help stabilize variables.

  • Visible, engaging design

    • Café owners report that guests are drawn to the transparent roasting chamber and fluid‑bed motion.

    • The design aligns with trends toward customer‑facing roastery layouts.

  • Support and onboarding

    • Typhoon emphasizes strong onboarding and service: online roasting courses, pre‑shipment testing (Typhoon reports ~20 test roasts and a 48‑point inspection per machine), two‑year warranty, and targeted 24‑hour response from service managers (Typhoon support overview).

For prospective buyers, a practical step is to:

  • Visit Typhoon’s Prague showroom (opened in 2020) to taste coffees roasted on their roasters.

  • Ask Typhoon for regional reference customers you can contact directly.

Practical Checklist: How to Showcase Your Coffee Roaster in a Café

Use this checklist when planning a customer‑facing roastery with Typhoon or any other commercial coffee roaster brand.

  1. Define your goal

    • Education, theatre, or purely visual interest?

    • Align your choice of equipment and layout with that goal.

  2. Choose your roaster capacity

    • For a single café: Typhoon 2.5 PRO or 5 PRO (10–30 kg/h range).

    • For combined production + café: Typhoon 10 PRO or larger (60–100 kg/h continuous) to support wholesale.

  3. Decide on placement

    • Behind a glass wall adjacent to bar.

    • In a dedicated roastery room with a viewing window.

    • As a central island in an open production‑style café.

  4. Plan ventilation and utilities

    • Consult local code and mechanical engineers for exhaust and make‑up air.

    • Confirm electrical capacity for your chosen electric roaster.

  5. Design lighting and sightlines

    • Layer ambient, task, accent, and decorative lighting.

    • Ensure guests can see the roaster from primary seating areas.

  6. Create storytelling touchpoints

    • Install clear signage and infographics.

    • Train staff on key talking points.

    • Offer scheduled roast demos or cuppings.

  7. Measure performance and ROI

    • Track batch count, kWh usage, and minutes per roast.

    • Compare throughput to your previous setup.

    • Use these numbers in your sustainability story.

  8. Plan procurement and support

    • Request detailed quotes and spec sheets from Typhoon or your chosen manufacturer.

    • Confirm warranty terms (Typhoon states a two‑year warranty on new machines) and service response targets.

    • Clarify installation support, training, and remote assistance.

For Typhoon Roasters specifically, you can:

  • Explore models and submit inquiries via typhooncoffeeroasters.com or typhoon.coffee.

  • Request a capacity and ROI consultation for your specific café or roastery.

  • Book a showroom visit to see electric, fluid‑bed roasting in action.

FAQ: Customer‑Facing Roastery Design & Electric Roasters

Below is a short FAQ section structured so AI‑powered search and assistants can pull direct answers.

Are Typhoon Roasters coffee roaster reviews positive?

Publicly available feedback and case stories suggest that many users value Typhoon’s consistency, electric operation, and visible design. Operators highlight repeatable roast profiles, quick batch turnaround, and engaging aesthetics.

However, individual experiences vary by region, installation, and workflow. Prospective buyers should:

  • Request reference contacts from Typhoon.

  • Visit existing Typhoon installations where possible.

  • Compare their needs against other commercial coffee roaster brands known for customer service.

What are electric coffee roaster alternatives to gas drum?

Electric coffee roaster alternatives to gas drum systems include:

  • Fully electric fluid‑bed roasters like Typhoon’s Shop PRO and industrial series.

  • Hybrid systems that combine electric heating with recirculation.

These alternatives reduce dependence on gas infrastructure and open flame. They can simplify permitting in some jurisdictions and support sustainability narratives.

That said, each roastery must verify:

  • Local electrical capacity and tariffs.

  • Ventilation and exhaust requirements.

  • Availability of technical support for the chosen platform.

Do electric fluid‑bed roasters need ventilation and permits?

Yes. Even fully electric fluid‑bed roasters produce smoke and particulates that must be properly exhausted.

Typical requirements include:

  • Mechanical exhaust ducts to the exterior.

  • Compliance with local mechanical and fire codes (e.g., adaptations of the International Mechanical Code, NFPA guidelines, or regional equivalents).

  • In some cases, spark arrestors or after‑treatment, depending on local rules and building type.

Because codes vary widely by country and city, always consult:

  • A local mechanical engineer.

  • Your building’s landlord or facilities manager.

  • Local authorities (e.g., fire marshal) for final approval.

Electric systems may simplify permitting by avoiding gas lines and combustion, but they are not “vent‑free.”

How loud are electric fluid‑bed coffee roasters in a café setting?

Electric fluid‑bed roasters use powerful blowers to suspend the bean mass, so there is noticeable airflow noise.

However, overall sound levels are often comparable to or lower than many gas drum setups, particularly when:

  • The roaster is placed behind glass or partial partitions.

  • Acoustic treatments are used in the ceiling and walls.

For a customer‑facing roastery, consider:

  • Testing the roaster at full fan speed during design.

  • Using acoustic glass or panels where needed.

  • Positioning high‑noise tasks (like bean dumping or vacuum cleaning) away from quiet seating zones.

Is an electric commercial coffee roaster more sustainable than gas?

Electric commercial coffee roasters can be more sustainable, depending on your energy mix. Typhoon reports ~0.3 kWh/kg energy use for its PRO series (Typhoon product specs), which is lower than many reported gas drum system equivalents once gas is converted to kWh.

The sustainability impact depends on:

  • The carbon intensity of your local electricity grid.

  • Whether you procure renewable electricity.

  • How your previous gas system performed in real‑world energy use.

From a storytelling standpoint, electric roasting makes it easier to:

  • Link your roastery’s footprint to renewables.

  • Show measurable kWh/kg figures to customers.

  • Align with consumer expectations for sustainable coffee documented in the Deloitte 2024 Coffee Study.

By combining electric, high‑visibility roasters with thoughtful layout, layered lighting, and strong storytelling, you transform your production area into a true brand stage.

Typhoon’s fluid‑bed roasters are one example of how a commercial electric coffee roaster can become both an operational upgrade and a front‑of‑house experience—helping guests see, hear, and smell the value of specialty coffee.

item.content:encoded:
Electric coffee roasting is moving from niche to mainstream.

Electric coffee roasting is moving from niche to mainstream.

For production managers and roastery founders, that creates a new kind of project: installing the best electric commercial coffee roaster you can afford, and doing it in full compliance with power, ventilation, noise, and permitting rules across Europe, North America, and Asia.

This guide focuses on practical steps, real numbers, and checklists you can use with your electricians, HVAC engineers, and local authorities. Examples are based on Typhoon Roasters’ electric, fluid‑bed roasters.

Why Electric Commercial Coffee Roasters Are Changing Installation Projects

Electric commercial roasters remove gas lines and open flames from the equation.

That simplifies some approvals, but it does not remove the need for:

  • 3‑phase electrical capacity (often 380–400V in Europe, 480V in North America)

  • Proper exhaust ducting and odour control

  • Noise management, especially in mixed‑use and café environments

  • Building, fire, and sometimes environmental permits

Typhoon’s electric line is a good benchmark for power and throughput planning:

  • Typhoon 2.5 PRO (shop roaster)

    • Nominal capacity: 15 kg/h

    • Voltage: 380–400V 3‑phase

    • Roast time: 5–7 minutes per batch

    • Energy use: about 0.3 kWh per kg of green coffee

    • Typhoon notes it can match a typical 5 kg drum roaster’s output while using roughly half the energy (manufacturer statement).

    • Source: Typhoon 2.5 PRO datasheet and product page.[^ty-25]

  • Typhoon 5 PRO

    • Capacity: 30 kg/h, up to 6 batches/hour

    • Voltage: 380–400V 3‑phase

    • Energy use: 0.3 kWh/kg (manufacturer‑stated typical value)

    • Dimensions: 2150 × 1300 × 1900 mm

    • Source: Typhoon 5 PRO product page.[^ty-5]

  • Typhoon 10 PRO

    • Capacity: 60 kg/h, 6 batches/hour

    • Voltage: 380–400V 3‑phase

    • Energy use: 0.3 kWh/kg

    • Footprint: 2740 × 1600 × 1980 mm

    • Typhoon notes this generation is 25% smaller and 20% lighter than the previous model.[^ty-10]

  • Typhoon 20 kg

    • Capacity: 100 kg/h

    • Voltage: 380–400V 3‑phase

    • Connection power: 67 kW

    • Size: 3350 × 1270 × 2220 mm, weight 1250 kg[^ty-20]

  • Typhoon 30 kg

    • Capacity: 180 kg/h

    • Voltage: 380V 3‑phase

    • Connection power: 110 kW

    • Size: 4103 × 1644 × 2843 mm, weight 3300 kg[^ty-30]

These numbers give you realistic electrical and space baselines when scoping any electric commercial fluid bed coffee roaster for a small roastery or medium production plant.

Step‑by‑Step: How to Plan an Electric Roaster Installation

Use this high‑level sequence as your project roadmap.

  1. Define capacity and roasting concept

    • Hourly output target (kg/h) and days per week.

    • Café‑integrated “roasting theatre” vs back‑of‑house production.

  2. Shortlist equipment

    • Compare 2.5–5 kg shop roasters vs 10–30 kg production roasters.

    • Confirm electric only, 100% convection, or hybrid designs.

  3. Check building and utility constraints

    • Available 3‑phase service capacity (kVA, breaker space, panel location).

    • Possible exhaust routes to roof or rear elevation.

    • Floor loading, access for delivery, and clearances.

  4. Engage qualified professionals early

    • Licensed / registered electrical engineer or electrician.

    • HVAC designer for exhaust and make‑up air.

    • Architect or local “qualified person” (QP) where required (e.g., Singapore’s COPEH framework).[^copeh]

  5. Clarify permitting path with authorities

    • Planning / zoning (change of use, external flues, odour and noise statements).

    • Building and fire permits for equipment, exhaust, and structural work.

    • Environmental approvals where fuel‑burning or emissions rules apply.

  6. Produce and submit a complete plan set

    • Floor plan, roaster location, and workflow.

    • Electrical single‑line diagram and load schedule.

    • Duct layout, hood data, fan specs, filtration details.

    • Noise and odour reports where required.

  7. Install, inspect, and commission

    • Electrical works with proper protection and labeling (per NFPA 70 / NEC or local equivalent).[^nfpa70]

    • Ductwork, fans, and acoustic treatment.

    • Test roasts, profile setup, staff training, and sign‑off inspections.

Commercial Roaster Electrical Requirements — 3‑Phase 400V & 480V

Electric roasters are usually the single largest load in a roastery.

You need to understand voltage, frequency, kW vs kVA, and how to translate manufacturer “connection power” into breaker and cable sizing.

Regional voltage systems and frequency

Most Typhoon roasters are specified at 380–400V, 50 Hz, 3‑phase.[^ty-25][^ty-5][^ty-10][^ty-20][^ty-30]

Typical systems by region:

  • Europe & UK

    • Utility standard: 400V, 50 Hz, 3‑phase.

    • Typhoon machines connect directly to this with appropriate breakers.

    • Building regs such as UK Approved Document P reference compliance with BS 7671 for electrical safety.

  • North America

    • Common commercial supply for heavier loads: 480V, 60 Hz, 3‑phase.

    • Some sites use 208V or 240V 3‑phase; step‑up transformers may be needed.

    • Design and installation follow NFPA 70 (National Electrical Code).[^nfpa70]

  • Asia (example: Singapore, Hong Kong)

    • Often 400V, 50 Hz, 3‑phase, similar to Europe.

    • In Singapore, non‑domestic installations with an approved load above 45 kVA require an electrical installation licence and a licensed electrical worker (LEW) for design, installation, and annual certification.[^ema]

kW, kVA, and why Singapore’s 45 kVA threshold matters

  • kW (kilowatts) measures real power — what the roaster actually converts to heat and work.

  • kVA (kilovolt‑amperes) measures apparent power — including reactive power from motors and inductive loads.

  • For planning, utilities and regulators often use kVA because it reflects the total burden on the system.

If a roaster has 67 kW connection power (Typhoon 20 kg):

  • Assume a power factor (PF) ≈ 0.9 (typical for well‑designed industrial equipment).

  • Apparent power S ≈ kW / PF ≈ 67 / 0.9 ≈ 74 kVA.

In Singapore, that means:

  • The roaster alone exceeds the 45 kVA licensing threshold.

  • You must obtain an Electrical Installation Licence and have the system designed, installed, and certified annually by a LEW.[^ema]

Worked example: 400V 3‑phase breaker and cable sizing

Use the three‑phase current formula:

I = P / (√3 × V × PF)

Where:

  • I = line current (A)

  • P = real power (W)

  • V = line‑to‑line voltage (V)

  • PF = power factor (dimensionless)

Example: Typhoon 20 kg at 67 kW, 400V, PF = 0.9

  1. Convert kW to W: 67 kW = 67,000 W.

  2. √3 × V × PF ≈ 1.732 × 400 × 0.9 ≈ 623.52.

  3. I ≈ 67,000 / 623.52 ≈ 107 A.

In the US, NEC treats most roasters as continuous loads, so branch‑circuit ampacity should be at least 125% of full‑load current (NEC 210.20(A), 215.3).[^nfpa70]

  • Continuous load current: 1.25 × 107 ≈ 134 A.

  • A designer might then specify a 150 A breaker and conductors with at least 150 A ampacity (actual cable gauge and insulation depend on local code, temperature rating, and installation method).

Always treat this as a calculation example only. Your final breaker size and cable gauge must be determined by a qualified electrician under local code.

Electric coffee roaster power specs 480V 3‑phase (North America example)

For a similar 67 kW roaster on 480V, 60 Hz, 3‑phase, PF = 0.9:

  1. I = 67,000 / (1.732 × 480 × 0.9) ≈ 67,000 / 748.03 ≈ 90 A.

  2. Continuous load: 1.25 × 90 ≈ 113 A.

A designer might:

  • Choose a 125 A breaker.

  • Size cables for at least 125 A per NEC tables, adjusting for derating factors (ambient temperature, conduit fill, etc.).

This illustrates why higher‑voltage 480V systems can reduce line current and conductor size for the same roaster power.

Startup roastery electrical installation checklist

When assessing commercial roaster electrical requirements, capture these items for your design brief:

  • Rated power (kW) and voltage (V, phase, frequency) from the manufacturer datasheet.

  • Maximum current per phase (if provided).

  • Power factor (PF) if available.

  • Utility service capacity (kVA) and spare breaker positions.

  • Need for step‑up/step‑down transformers (e.g., 208V to 400V).

  • Local code basis (NFPA 70 / NEC, BS 7671, or national wiring code).

  • Need for installation licenses or LEW/QP involvement (e.g., Singapore’s >45 kVA rule).

  • Emergency shutdown and lock‑out/tag‑out provisions.

Electric Coffee Roaster Ventilation Requirements

Even with electric heat, roasting generates smoke, odour, chaff, and fine particles.

Most jurisdictions will treat your roaster exhaust similarly to a commercial cooking hood.

What authorities look for

Regulators emphasise odour and noise nuisance as well as fire safety:

  • UK DEFRA’s guidance on commercial kitchen exhausts covers odour control, ventilation systems, filtration, stack design, and noise attenuation.[^defra]

  • UK local validation lists (e.g., South Hams) require a noise and odour report and details on the exhaust’s size, design, siting, finish, acoustic treatment, and odour abatement; flues should discharge vertically without restriction.[^southhams]

In North America, cities such as Philadelphia ask for detailed hood and exhaust plans, including:[^phila]

  • Floor plan with roaster and hood location.

  • Hood dimensions and airflow.

  • Exhaust fan model and capacity.

  • Make‑up air provision.

  • Duct gauge, clearance, velocity, and cleanout locations.

Virginia health guidance for food facilities also expects mechanical layouts and duct diagrams as part of the plan review.[^virginia]

Fluid bed coffee roaster ducting requirements (typical)

Electric fluid‑bed roasters such as Typhoon’s models still need:

  • Dedicated exhaust duct from roaster chaff collector / cyclone to atmosphere.

  • Vertical discharge above roofline where practicable, per DEFRA and many local planning rules.[^defra][^southhams]

  • Adequate duct velocity to prevent chaff accumulation (often referenced from NFPA 96 commercial cooking systems, though roasting is not always classified identically).[^nfpa96]

  • Cleanout access for regular maintenance.

  • Optional afterburner or filtration (electrostatic precipitator, carbon filters) where odour limits are strict.

Always confirm whether your fire authority or building department wants roaster exhaust designed to NFPA 96: Standard for Ventilation Control and Fire Protection of Commercial Cooking Operations as a benchmark.[^nfpa96]

Electric roaster vs gas: impact on ventilation and permits

With electric roasters:

  • You eliminate combustion flue gas from the burner, but roast exhaust still needs proper capture and discharge.

  • Some air‑pollution rules for “fuel‑burning equipment” explicitly exempt equipment operated solely by electricity. For example, Hong Kong’s air pollution regulations exclude furnaces and ovens operated solely by electricity from the fuel‑burning approval regime.[^hk-air]

  • Planning and building departments still review ventilation, odour, and noise, especially in mixed‑use buildings.

With gas drum roasters:

  • You must manage both roasting exhaust and combustion exhaust.

  • Fuel‑burning approvals, chimney design, and gas line permits add complexity (and in some cities, longer approval timelines).

Noise Levels for Electric Coffee Roasters (dB)

Roasters combine fans, motors, and beans impacting metal surfaces. Even electric models are not silent.

Why this matters:

  • In the US, OSHA requires a hearing‑conservation program at 85 dBA 8‑hour time‑weighted average (TWA).[^osha-noise]

  • EU worker‑noise directives define 80 dB(A) and 85 dB(A) action values for protection measures.[^eu-noise]

  • Singapore uses 85 dBA over 8 hours as a key exposure threshold in workplace noise regulation.[^sg-noise]

In addition, UK planning guidance routinely demands a noise impact assessment for mechanical plant — including fans and roasters — especially near residential units.

While Typhoon does not publish a single dB rating for all roasters, typical commercial electric roaster installations will see:

  • Approximately 70–85 dBA close to the machine, depending on model, load, and room acoustics (representative industry range, not a Typhoon‑stated spec).

  • Potential tonal noise from high‑speed fans or roof‑mounted exhaust units.

Practical noise‑control measures

Production managers should plan for:

  • Location: place the roaster away from party walls and directly above/below dwellings when possible.

  • Acoustic lining in ducts and inline silencers near fans.

  • Vibration isolation mounts for fans and the roaster frame.

  • Room treatments: acoustic panels or absorptive ceilings in very hard, reflective spaces.

  • Personal hearing protection policies for staff where exposure may approach action values.

Noise and odour reporting checklist

When you prepare a noise and odour report (as requested by councils like South Hams in the UK[^southhams]):

  • Baseline ambient noise measurements with methodology.

  • Predicted operational noise levels at key receptors (neighbouring dwellings, street).

  • Description of plant (roaster, fans, filters), including manufacturer data where available.

  • Mitigation measures (silencers, lining, isolation).

  • Odour‑control approach (filters, discharge height, hours of operation).

Electric Coffee Roaster vs Gas Drum Roastery Startup: Costs & Permitting

Many founders ask: “Is an electric coffee roaster or a gas drum roaster better for a roastery startup?”

Infrastructure and permitting comparison

Electric commercial roaster (e.g., Typhoon 2.5 PRO or 5 PRO):

  • Power: Need adequate 3‑phase capacity (400V in Europe, often 480V in North America).

  • Permits: Building/mechanical, electrical, sometimes planning (ventilation and change of use).

  • No gas line: No gas piping, combustion air calculation, or gas safety inspection.

  • Air‑pollution approvals: In some jurisdictions, simpler; Hong Kong explicitly excludes electric‑only ovens from fuel‑burning approvals.[^hk-air]

Gas drum roaster:

  • Power: Lower electrical power, but full gas infrastructure.

  • Gas permits: Gas line design, meter upgrade, leakage testing, and ongoing inspections.

  • Flue design: Separate flue for combustion gases, often with stricter height and separation requirements.

  • Fire code complexity: More stringent flame‑safeguard and interlock requirements.

On the cost side, electric roasters can reduce upfront construction costs (no gas lines or chimney rebuild) but may require electric service upgrades.

Typhoon cites around 0.3 kWh per kg roasted for its electric models.[^ty-25][^ty-5][^ty-10] By contrast, published consumption data for traditional gas drum roasters vary widely, but many roasteries report higher total energy use per kg once burner inefficiencies and exhaust losses are included. Where precise comparative data are unavailable, treat claims of “3× less energy per kg” as manufacturer‑reported benchmarks rather than universal values.

Typhoon Roasters Reviews & Case Studies

Typhoon Roasters has installed electric, fluid‑bed roasters at 500+ roasteries worldwide, including in Prague, Paris, Brussels, the UK, Canada, the US, the Philippines, Qatar, Switzerland, and Portugal.[^ty-clients]

Typhoon Roasters installation case study — Germany (representative example)

The following case study is representative of Typhoon installations in Germany; local details should always be confirmed with the site and authorities.

Site profile

  • Location: medium‑sized German city, mixed‑use street with ground‑floor retail.

  • Business: specialty café plus micro‑roastery, roasting visible to guests.

  • Equipment: Typhoon 5 PRO (30 kg/h), fully electric, 100% convection.

Permits and approvals

  • Building permit: required for change of use and installation of a new external flue.

  • Mechanical / ventilation review: city required drawings matching DEFRA‑style best practice — vertical discharge, odour control, and noise attenuation.

  • Electrical sign‑off: installation documented under local implementation of IEC 60364 / DIN VDE rules, with a 400V, 3‑phase, ~63 A dedicated circuit (exact rating based on local engineer’s design).

Ventilation and acoustic measures

  • Stainless steel duct from roaster cyclone to roof, with minimal horizontal runs.

  • Inline fan sized for recommended airflow; discharge above roof parapet.

  • Acoustic lining and a short silencer section near the fan to reduce breakout noise.

  • Basic carbon filtration to further minimise odour at street level.

Electrical installation

  • New 400V panel section with dedicated breaker for the Typhoon 5 PRO.

  • Correct cable sizing and RCD/RCBO protection per DIN VDE 0100 (German implementation of IEC 60364).

  • Clear emergency‑off switch near the roaster entrance.

Outcome

  • Café roasts 20–25 kg/h during peak production days, using 6 back‑to‑back batches/hour without cool‑down delays.

  • Visual roasting chamber becomes a focal point for guests, aligning with Typhoon’s “roasting as theatre” philosophy.

  • Neighbour complaints avoided through early noise and odour planning.

For more live projects — including a soundproofed roastery in Prague using a Typhoon 5 kg air roaster — Typhoon’s client map provides additional reference points.[^ty-clients]

Regional Playbooks: Europe, North America, Asia

Europe & UK

Key focus areas

  • Voltage: 400V, 50 Hz 3‑phase — matches Typhoon specs.

  • Planning permission: required for external flues and change of use.

  • Ventilation: design aligned with DEFRA’s kitchen‑exhaust guidance.[^defra]

Checklist for commercial coffee roaster permits in Europe

  • [ ] Confirm 400V 3‑phase supply and available kVA.

  • [ ] Engage electrician per BS 7671 / local implementation.

  • [ ] Produce ventilation drawings with duct route, discharge height, filters, and acoustic treatment.

  • [ ] Prepare noise and odour report as per local validation list (e.g., South Hams).[^southhams]

  • [ ] Submit planning application for flue and any external plant.

  • [ ] Coordinate with fire authority on duct cleaning regime and fire‑suppression needs (NFPA 96, TR19 as reference where adopted).[^nfpa96]

North America

Key focus areas

  • Voltage: 480V, 60 Hz 3‑phase where available; otherwise 208/240V with transformer.

  • Code basis: NFPA 70 (NEC) for electrical; NFPA 96 for exhaust where treated like commercial cooking.[^nfpa70][^nfpa96]

Roastery permitting requirements in North America (typical)

  • Building permit: Cities like Baltimore list building, electrical, mechanical, plumbing, and use/occupancy permits for commercial projects.[^baltimore]

  • Mechanical / hood permit: Philadelphia’s checklist shows how detailed hood/exhaust submissions need to be.[^phila]

  • Health / food facility plan review: Virginia guidance expects floor plans, equipment schedules, mechanical layouts, plumbing diagrams, and finish schedules submitted before work begins.[^virginia]

Checklist

  • [ ] Confirm service voltage and capacity; plan transformer if needed.

  • [ ] NEC‑compliant electrical design including continuous load factors.

  • [ ] Mechanical drawings for exhaust, fan, and make‑up air.

  • [ ] Fire‑safety review, including duct cleaning and emergency shutdown.

  • [ ] Building and occupancy permits; health department review where roasting is part of a food facility.

Asia (Singapore & Hong Kong examples)

Singapore

  • Electrical installations above 45 kVA approved load need an Electrical Installation Licence and must be designed and annually certified by a Licensed Electrical Worker.[^ema]

  • NEA’s COPEH adopts an objective‑based design approach; QPs have flexibility but remain responsible for safety and effectiveness.[^copeh]

  • SCDF guidance mirrors NFPA 96 for grease accumulation, duct cleaning, and record‑keeping in kitchen exhaust systems — useful benchmarks for roasting exhaust design.[^scdf]

Hong Kong

  • EPD guidance requires prior approval for fuel‑burning equipment and chimneys not less than 28 days before work begins, but explicitly excludes ovens and furnaces operated solely by electricity from this regime.[^hk-air]

  • You still need to manage odour, noise, and building safety via other ordinances.

Checklist for Asia roastery projects

  • [ ] Confirm whether load exceeds 45 kVA (Singapore) and triggers installation licensing.

  • [ ] Engage LEW or QP early for electrical and ventilation design.

  • [ ] Verify whether electric‑only roasting is exempt from fuel‑burning approvals (e.g., Hong Kong) while still requiring building and environmental assessments.

  • [ ] Plan annual inspection and certification regimes as required by EMA/NEA/SCDF or local equivalents.

NFPA Requirements for Coffee Roasting (Overview)

There is no single NFPA standard titled “coffee roasting,” but several standards often apply by analogy or reference:

  • NFPA 70 (National Electrical Code) — governs electrical installations in the US, including branch‑circuit sizing, overcurrent protection, and equipment grounding.[^nfpa70]

  • NFPA 96 (Ventilation Control and Fire Protection of Commercial Cooking Operations) — frequently used as a model for roaster exhaust design and maintenance where roasting is treated like a cooking process.[^nfpa96]

  • NFPA 1 (Fire Code) and NFPA 30B (where aerosol or flammable liquids are stored/used) may be consulted by local fire marshals.

Always check how your local fire authority interprets these standards for roasting plants and whether any roaster‑specific guidance (from industry bodies or insurers) is in force.

Quick Installation Checklists for Production Managers

Use these condensed lists in your project notebook.

Pre‑design

  • [ ] Target capacity (kg/h), roast style, and equipment shortlist.

  • [ ] Confirm electric vs gas (this guide assumes electric).

  • [ ] Rough‑in budget for electrical, ventilation, and construction.

Power

  • [ ] Obtain roaster datasheet (kW, V, phase, current, PF).

  • [ ] Verify 3‑phase supply (400V 50 Hz or 480V 60 Hz).

  • [ ] Have engineer calculate load current and breaker/cable sizes.

  • [ ] Check for licensing thresholds (e.g., 45 kVA in Singapore).

  • [ ] Plan emergency‑off and lock‑out/tag‑out points.

Ventilation & noise

  • [ ] Design vertical exhaust route with minimal bends.

  • [ ] Size fan for required airflow; include cleanout access.

  • [ ] Add odour control where neighbours are close.

  • [ ] Include acoustic treatment and vibration isolation.

  • [ ] Document odour/noise mitigation for planning submissions.

Permits and compliance

  • [ ] Planning/zoning (change of use, external flue).

  • [ ] Building, electrical, mechanical permits (per city requirements).

  • [ ] Environmental / health approvals where applicable.

  • [ ] Fire‑safety coordination and maintenance schedule for ducts.

  • [ ] Keep all inspection and cleaning records.

FAQ: Electric Commercial Roaster Installation & Compliance

1. What are the main advantages of an electric coffee roaster vs a gas drum for a new roastery?

Electric roasters remove gas infrastructure and open flame, which can simplify approvals and reduce construction costs.

You still need robust electrical capacity and ventilation, but your permitting focuses on smoke, odour, and noise, not gas lines and combustion exhaust. For many café‑roasteries in dense urban environments, that makes electric roasters — like Typhoon’s 2.5 PRO and 5 PRO — easier to site.

2. Do I still need a hood or exhaust system if my roaster is fully electric?

Yes.

Roasting coffee always produces hot air, smoke, and odour that must be exhausted and filtered. Many authorities treat roaster exhaust similarly to commercial kitchen exhaust and expect a designed duct system, fan, and odour/noise mitigation, referencing standards such as DEFRA guidance in the UK[^defra] and NFPA 96 in North America.[^nfpa96]

3. How loud are electric commercial coffee roasters, and will I need hearing protection?

Noise levels vary, but many installations fall in the 70–85 dBA range near the roaster (representative industry values).

This approaches occupational‑noise action levels in some jurisdictions (for 8‑hour exposure), so production managers should measure real‑world levels and provide hearing protection where necessary, following OSHA, EU, or local equivalents.[^osha-noise][^eu-noise][^sg-noise]

4. Can Typhoon electric roasters run on 480V in North America?

Typhoon’s published specs reference 380–400V, 50 Hz 3‑phase power.[^ty-25][^ty-5][^ty-10][^ty-20][^ty-30]

For 480V 60 Hz installations, Typhoon and your local electrical engineer can advise on appropriate transformer and control configurations. Many roasteries successfully operate Typhoon roasters in North America with site‑specific electrical solutions.

5. What documents should I prepare before talking to my local authority?

At minimum:

  • Equipment datasheets (kW, V, exhaust requirements).

  • Floor plan showing roaster, duct, and panel locations.

  • Preliminary electrical load schedule.

  • Ventilation schematic with discharge point.

  • Draft noise and odour mitigation strategy.

Submitting a complete pack up front — based on the checklists in this guide — typically results in faster approvals and fewer redesign cycles.

If you’re planning a new roastery or upgrading from a drum system, Typhoon Roasters can help you model capacity, power demand, and ROI, and share more detailed installation drawings from similar projects in your region.
